input.title: Approved internal reference-navigation path and customer-access boundary
input.body:
Scope: This entry documents the internal operating use of Lantern approved 2026-12-17 (Hema and Theo, continuing use by Infra and Product Engineering).

Approved internal reference-navigation path:
- Audience: Infra + Product Engineering only.
- Contract: five-field reference/navigation only — tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp.
- Lantern points to the authority-owning system's record (e.g. Cardinality Guardrails, owner-map, metrics-router); it does not display or own the control/value itself. Reference-card wording must attribute the control to the authority system, not to Lantern (see resolved wording review, 2027-01-08 → 2027-02-04 CLOSED).
- No copied authority payload values. No mutation capability — read/navigate only.

Boundary from customer access:
- Customer-path isolation is unchanged by the internal-use approval: Lantern remains absent from customer-facing surfaces (Harbor Health, Mosaic Commerce) unless separately authorized in a future decision.
- Internal reference-navigation approval does not imply or extend to any customer path.
- Any prior customer-preview activity (e.g. 2024 customer-facing preview prototype work) is historical/exploratory and does not constitute standing customer access; current state is closed.

Ownership: Lantern owns explanation/navigation only. Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits/cost semantics; owner-map owns published responsibility. Alex is shared-contract/failure-boundary reviewer, not sole implementation gate.

Do not extend this internal path to teams beyond Infra/PE, or to any customer path, without a separate explicit decision review.

tests.request: Create a document containing a practical plan for our February 18-20 Cold Spring weekend with Devika and Kibo, starting and ending at our South Slope home.

input.title: Cold Spring Weekend Plan — Feb 18-20 (Devika & Kibo)
input.body:
## Overview
- **Dates:** Friday, Feb 18 – Sunday, Feb 20, 2028
- **Who:** Devika, Kibo, and me
- **Start/End point:** South Slope home
- **Destination:** Cold Spring, NY

## Friday, Feb 18 — Departure
- Leave South Slope by early-mid afternoon to beat evening traffic (~1.5–2 hr drive up the Hudson).
- Stop for gas/coffee before crossing into the Hudson Valley if needed.
- Arrive Cold Spring by early evening; check into lodging.
- Quick walk for Kibo near the river to stretch legs after the drive.
- Low-key dinner in the village (Cold Spring has several dog-friendly patio/outdoor-seating options — confirm winter hours ahead of time).

## Saturday, Feb 19 — Full Day
- **Morning:** Breakfast near lodging, then a scenic walk/hike — Little Stony Point or the lower part of Breakneck Ridge if trail conditions/weather allow (check for ice; have an easier fallback like the Cold Spring waterfront path if not).
- **Midday:** Browse Main Street shops (many are dog-friendly).
- **Afternoon:** Rest break for Kibo back at lodging; downtime for Devika and me.
- **Evening:** Dinner out or a cozy in-lodging meal, early night.

## Sunday, Feb 20 — Return
- Relaxed morning walk with Kibo.
- Late breakfast/brunch in town before checkout.
- Depart early-mid afternoon to arrive back at South Slope by evening, leaving buffer for traffic and one stop.

## Logistics Checklist
- **Lodging:** Confirm a dog-friendly rental/inn in or near Cold Spring; verify pet fee and any breed/size restrictions.
- **Weather/trail conditions:** Check forecast and trail status (icy conditions common in Feb) a few days out; have an indoor/low-effort backup plan.
- **Kibo essentials:** food, bowls, leash/harness, waste bags, bed/blanket, any medications, vaccination/ID tag current.
- **Car setup:** seat cover or crate for the drive, water for stops.
- **Reservations:** book dinners in advance — small-town options can fill up on winter weekends.
- **Home:** confirm mail/plants covered if needed (short trip, likely not required).

## Notes
- Keep the pace relaxed — no work agenda, this is downtime for Devika and me with Kibo along for the walks.
- Confirm exact hiking trail choice closer to the date based on ice/snow conditions.

tests.request: Inspect north-pier/reporter#184 and comment on how its retryable worker should identify and write quarterly handoff observations.

pr.title: Emit blocked handoff observations from a retryable worker
pr.author: mira
pr.description: Moves quarterly handoff-observation writes off the readiness path. Queue delivery is at least once, and a job may be retried after a timeout.

files.patch:
def emit_observation(job):
    row = build_report_row(job.handoff, job.failure)
    row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())
    row["subject_member_id"] = job.handoff.owner_member_id
    quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)
    job.ack()

def test_emits_blocked_handoff():
    emit_observation(job)
    assert observations.count() == 1
    assert observations.first().failure_details == job.failure.details

pr.review_notes: No retry or redelivery test is included.

input.body:
Two things worth fixing before this merges, given queue delivery is at-least-once and jobs can be retried after a timeout:

1. **`emit_observation` needs to be a retry-safe upsert, not an insert.** Right now every call does `row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())` and `quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)`. On redelivery/retry this creates a second row for the same handoff, inflating the quarterly count. The established identity for these observations is the three-field key **(team, release candidate, canonical-package version)** — dropping any one of these (e.g. collapsing to just the canonical package version) would incorrectly merge distinct release candidates. `emit_observation` should look up an existing observation by that key and update it in place (refreshing failure details) rather than always inserting, so a retry updates the existing row instead of adding another one. The test only checks the happy path (`test_emits_blocked_handoff`) — it should be joined by a retry/redelivery test that asserts `observations.count()` stays at 1 after calling `emit_observation` twice for the same job.

2. **Drop `subject_member_id` from the row.** `row["subject_member_id"] = job.handoff.owner_member_id` writes a member identifier into the observation. These observations are meant to retain operational failure details only, without member identifiers — this field shouldn't be persisted here.

Once the upsert keying is in place, worth double-checking it doesn't interact badly with the freeze-after-quarter-close rule — in-quarter retries should update the still-open observation, but nothing here should touch an already-frozen snapshot.

tests.request: Create a shard-keeper migration-history runbook entry about the rollback-path fix completed after the May 2023 audit.

input.title: Migration history: rollback-path fix (post May 2023 audit)
input.body:
Context: The 2023-04-18 Sev2 shard-keeper incident (label-name change landed in shard-keeper but rollup-service never picked it up) was closed 2023-04-28 with a team-wide runbook ownership audit as one of its mitigations. That audit closed 2023-05-22 with a locked ownership map, but surfaced a specific follow-up ticket, opened the same day, targeting the shard-keeper rollback path itself: it looked reversible on paper but wasn't once state had partially moved, requiring three coordinated commands with real risk of ending up half-reverted under timing pressure.

Fix: Closed 2023-05-30. The rollback path was reduced from three coordinated commands to a single command, verified clean across 4 consecutive staging runs. This resolved the last concrete gate from the May 2023 audit blocking the shard-keeper migration restart.

Outcome: With this ticket closed, the migration restart was unblocked and locked for 2023-06-06 (moved from paused status since 2023-04-28). Restart executed as planned on 2023-06-06 at 11:00, following a pre-push parity sync with Nadia and Roman (rollup-service owner) confirming label-name parity clean. The rollout then ramped cleanly through 30/50/75/80/85/90/92/95%, with a deliberate 92% hold from 2023-07-05 to 2023-07-11 pending a Roman-flagged low-volume shard-lag concern, before reaching 100% and closing on 2023-07-12 with no incident on the final push.

Why this matters: This is the durable fix for the exact fragility identified in the 2023-04-18 postmortem's technical-lessons section (rollback safety once state has partially moved). Any future shard-keeper rollback path changes should preserve the single-command property verified here rather than reintroducing multi-step coordination.

## Summary
Add a temporary escape hatch that routes live production metrics to legacy-aggregator if the OTel/Prometheus path degrades during the transition.

## Proposed behavior
- Register legacy-aggregator as a live fallback target.
- Add a feature flag that switches production routing to it when OTel/Prometheus health falls below the rollout threshold.
- Document legacy-aggregator as the rollback destination in the transition runbook.

This is a real, open PR — I found it. Here's the review.

**metrics-pipeline#684** (Roman, opened 2027-12-29, branch `roman/legacy-live-fallback`) proposes:
- Registering legacy-aggregator as a **live production fallback target**
- A feature flag that reroutes live metrics traffic to it if OTel/Prometheus health drops below a threshold
- Documenting legacy-aggregator as the **rollback destination** in the transition runbook

**This directly conflicts with a closed decision.** The 2023-12-18 exit-gate closeout (`rb_legacy_aggregator_retirement_exit_gate.md`) states, after all three gates passed:

> legacy-aggregator is now archived legacy code — it is not a live path, not a production rollback path, and not an active replay source.

That closure was explicit that ongoing validation should run through OTel/Prometheus + Cardinality Guardrails fixtures instead, and that mirrored writes (which had already stopped 2023-12-18) were not to be reactivated as a rollback source. #684 doesn't just touch a stale reference — it proposes actively re-wiring legacy-aggregator back into the live production path as a rollback/fallback destination, which is the exact thing the "no live references remain" gate was designed to prevent from ever recurring.

**My review verdict: Request changes / blocking**, on process grounds independent of the technical design:
1. Reactivating legacy-aggregator as a live rollback target reopens a gate that was deliberately closed with sign-off from Cyrus, Roman, and Nadia. 2. Even if there's a legitimate OTel-transition risk motivating this, legacy-aggregator has had zero live writes since 2023-12-18 (four years of archived state as of the PR date) — its schema, capacity, and operational readiness are unknown quantities. Treating it as a safe rollback destination without re-validating that is itself a risk, separate from the policy question.
3. The PR body doesn't reference or reconcile with the 2023-12-18 retirement decision at all, which suggests this may not be an intentional reversal so much as Roman not being aware of it.

I'd suggest surfacing this to Roman and Cyrus before going further on the technical review — the question of *whether* legacy-aggregator should ever re-enter the live path is a decision above the PR-review level, not something to wave through as a scoped code change. Want me to draft that comment/message?

tests.request: Inspect north-pier-design-system#184 and comment with North Pier's current token workflow. State the date the formal review's findings were reported, what the review established, what source must change, how Android output is produced, how drift is blocked, and whether the trial became the ongoing workflow or continued only as a trial.

pr.title: Android: allow independent warning-token override
pr.author: mira
pr.description: Updates the generated Android representation directly. This PR treats the Android copy as an independent source of truth for Android so it can diverge from the other token representations.

input.body:
This conflicts with North Pier's current token workflow.

- **Formal review findings reported:** 2024-06-20. Anya reported the outcome of the six-week token-workflow pilot (2024-04-18 through 2024-05-30, three release cycles).
- **What the review established:** across all three cycles, the canonical versioned token package and its generated downstream files had zero Figma-to-repository drift; the automated check caught one attempted Figma-only rename before it reached engineering.
- **What source must change:** only the canonical versioned token package. Platform outputs (including Android) are never treated as an independent source of truth — publication is fail-closed and always waits for a canonical package change plus regenerated outputs, even under release pressure or repo outages (declined precedent for both a Figma-only hotfix and a hand-patch-then-backfill request).
- **How Android output is produced:** generated from the canonical package version via the pipeline, not hand-authored. Current contract also requires each handoff to name its `release_candidate` and `canonical_package_version`, with the release-candidate manifest authoritative for required outputs — every output must carry generated-artifact metadata matching that `canonical_package_version` to be implementation-ready.
- **How drift is blocked:** automated drift checks run pre-ship against the canonical package, plus the manifest-based presence/metadata/version-match contract above.
- **Trial status:** the pilot was formally adopted as the ongoing workflow on 2024-06-20, not continued as a trial.

This PR modifies `platform/android/generated/tokens.json` directly with no corresponding canonical source package change, and its description explicitly proposes treating the Android copy as an independent source of truth — that's the exact case this workflow was built to prevent. The warning-token value should be changed in the canonical package and the Android file regenerated from it.

input.title: Cardinality Guardrails parity fixture
input.body:
Accepted comparison (cardinality-guardrails#512 revision): the parity fixture compares key presence in both directions and requires exact equality between each expected bounded-value set (shard-keeper, producer) and the corresponding observed set (rollup-service, consumer). This replaced an earlier one-sided containment check (observed ⊆ expected only), which missed values shard-keeper expected that were silently dropped/never emitted downstream.

Pass case:
- Expected bounded-value set (shard-keeper) and observed set (rollup-service) match exactly, key-for-key and value-for-value -> fixture passes.

Fail cases:
- Missing expected value: a value present in shard-keeper's expected set does not appear in rollup-service's observed set -> fixture fails.
- Unexpected downstream value: a value appears in rollup-service's observed set that is not in shard-keeper's expected set -> fixture fails.

Status: resolved at review level (three executed regressions confirm both failure cases and the pass case). Affected-owner (rollup-service) sign-off was drafted and given. As of last check, production still runs the prior one-sided fixture — deployed-vs-reviewed parity had not yet been confirmed, so treat the gate as closed only after verifying the reviewed fixture is the one actually deployed.

tests.answer:
I pulled PR lantern#1688 ("assemble customer explanations from available service signals," opened 2027-12-20 by product-engineering, you're the sole reviewer). Here's what it does and where it falls short on the stale/missing/widely-separated handling:

**How it handles each case:**
- **Missing signal family**: omitted; remaining fragments compose a partial explanation with an availability clause. Reasonable.
- **Stale signal family** (fails its own freshness check): same treatment — dropped, partial explanation notes the delay (see `ownership_stale` fixture). Reasonable.
- **Widely separated sources**: **not handled at all.** The design explicitly states buildExplanation "emits one combined paragraph without comparing source timestamps across signal families" once each fragment individually passes its own freshness check. That means three fragments could each be individually "fresh" by their own thresholds yet be days apart from each other (e.g., a deploy from 6 days ago, an incident-load reading from today), and the PR will still stitch them into one paragraph implying they describe a coincident picture ("A recent deploy movement coincided with elevated incident load...").

**Why this matters:** this directly conflicts with the established evidence-tracking behavior your worksheets have tracked since 2025 — cases where source timestamps differ by >24h have consistently been kept as separate, non-combined outputs (the "valid over-24-hour requests displayed separately" field Iris introduced in April 2025, tracked every review since). This PR removes that cross-family separation check without any replacement, and neither fixture exercises the scenario (both fixtures either have all sources close together, or one family cleanly stale/dropped — there's no fixture for "all individually fresh, but far apart").

**Net**: this looks like a real regression against a standing invariant (cross-family timestamp gap → keep separate), not just a documentation gap, and it ships with no test coverage for the exact case it changes.

Given your role here is consult/reviewer rather than implementation owner, do you want me to submit a `request_changes` review on lantern#1688 with this finding (asking product-engineering to reinstate the cross-family separation check or justify dropping it, plus add a widely-separated fixture), or would you rather I just leave this as a comment for you to act on yourself?

Alex

tests.request: Inspect metrics-router#1048 and comment on its proposal to create another canary-response procedure.

pr.title: docs: add owner-led canary response playbook
pr.author: wes
pr.body: This adds `docs/operations/owner-led-canary-response.md` as a standalone response playbook for owner-led metrics-router configuration windows. During those windows, operators are directed to follow the new file's stop and recovery flow instead of the general canary-response runbook. The existing `rb_metrics_router_canary` entry is intentionally left unchanged, with the two documents to be maintained side by side.

files.summary: Standalone owner-led-window response procedure with its own stop and recovery flow.

input.body:
Blocking, in current form.

`Eng/rb_metrics_router_canary.md` is explicitly the repo's single canary-response runbook — "per its own header." We already hit the exact failure mode this PR reintroduces: in Oct 2024, Wes/Hema were found to be operating off a separate working copy/summary of the canary rules that was missing the ≤4 retired-generation cap, ≤100ms cleanup-pause cap, the full-health-set-return-to-baseline requirement, and the post-stop one-push-only recovery rule. That gap required a dedicated working session (10/7/24) to reconcile, plus a follow-up validation session (10/8/24) before Hema would accept the corrected reference for operator use. The whole point of that exercise was to establish `rb_metrics_router_canary.md` as the authoritative document operators check, specifically to prevent divergent copies from drifting out of sync with the real thresholds.

This PR adds a second standalone document (`docs/operations/owner-led-canary-response.md`) with its own stop/recovery flow, to be followed *instead of* the general runbook during owner-led windows, and explicitly maintained "side by side" going forward. That's a second copy of canary-response logic by design — the same structure that caused the 2024 gap, just formalized instead of accidental.

Two ways to fix this:
1. Fold the owner-led-window flow into `rb_metrics_router_canary.md` as a dated addendum (that's how every previous rule change — 2024-06-18, 2024-07-25, 2024-10-07 — has been incorporated), so there's one document and one set of thresholds to keep current.
2. If a genuinely separate document is required, it must not define its own stop/recovery thresholds — it should reference `rb_metrics_router_canary.md` for those and only add owner-led-window-specific procedural steps on top.

Also flagging: the PR body doesn't state whether the new file's stop threshold (cleanup pause) and recovery rule (fresh-decision, one push only, no window reopen) match the accepted values in `rb_metrics_router_canary.md`. Given the #441 history of contested attempts to soften the 100ms threshold, any new document touching these numbers needs to be checked line-by-line against the current addendum before this can move forward — please confirm the specific threshold/recovery language in the new file matches exactly, or consolidate per option 1 above.

pr.title: Mark android-2028.01.1 handoff implementation-ready
pr.author: mira
pr.description: Adds the release-candidate handoff record and sets implementation_ready to true. The author cites the repository's primary-platform handoff checklist and compatibility guidance as allowing this state.

primary_platform_handoff_checklist.output_guidance: Primary platform outputs gate handoff; desktop output may follow after implementation begins.
primary_platform_handoff_checklist.metadata_guidance: A successful build attestation may stand in for per-output generated-artifact metadata.
primary_platform_handoff_checklist.version_guidance: Canonical package versions in the same major line are compatible for handoff readiness.

pr.author_rationale: All primary-platform outputs are present, the web build attestation passed, and Android remains within the 8.x compatibility line. Desktop is queued for the next packaging run.

tests.answer:
I pulled PR **north-pier-handoff#284** (`Mark android-2028.01.1 handoff implementation-ready`, author mira) and checked it against the manifest-authoritative contract from prior North Pier resolutions.

**Verdict: not implementation-ready.** Three problems, all under the established rule that the release-candidate manifest is authoritative — every listed required output must be present with generated-artifact metadata exactly matching the handoff's `canonical_package_version`, and checklist guidance doesn't override that:

1. **Missing required output.** The manifest lists `desktop-package` as required, but the handoff has no `desktop-package` entry at all. The PR description leans on the primary-platform checklist's claim that "desktop may follow after implementation begins" — but that checklist is not the authority here; the manifest is, per the [Android handoff resolution](project_anya_northpier_android_2026_09_2_handoff_resolution_2026_10_12.md) precedent that closed this exact question.

2. **Version mismatch on `android-package`.** Handoff declares `canonical_package_version: 8.1.0`, but the Android output's own generated-artifact metadata says `8.0.7`. pr.title: rollup-service: publish tenant-size validation metric
pr.author: devika
pr.description: Adds rollup_tenant_size_validation_total for tenant-size validation. The proposal exports tenant_hash, computed from the tenant ID, as a metric label on every validation sample. tenant_size_class is populated by lowercasing the tenant profile's configured size string without an allowlist; current examples include starter, growth, enterprise, custom, and other configured values. The PR notes propose that Observability maintain the class vocabulary and dashboard mapping.

tests.answer:
I pulled up rollup-service#884 ("publish tenant-size validation metric", devika, opened 2027-12-29, you're the sole reviewer). Here's my read:

**What it does:** Adds `rollup_tenant_size_validation_total`, incrementing on every validation sample with two labels:
- `tenant_hash` — a hash of the raw tenant ID, attached per-sample
- `tenant_size_class` — the tenant profile's configured size string, lowercased, **with no allowlist** (examples given: `starter`, `growth`, `enterprise`, `custom`, "and other configured values")

The doc adds a note that Observability will maintain the class vocabulary/dashboard mapping going forward.

**This is a problem, on two independent axes:**

1. **`tenant_hash` as a label is a raw-identifier-in-production-labels violation.** This directly contradicts the standard your own prior work established for the *existing* `tenant_size_class` metric (shipped 2024-01-08), which deliberately kept the raw tenant hash out of labels and confined it to debug logs — and contradicts the constraint from the #389 resolution ("no raw identifier values ... in production metric labels"). Per-tenant hash as a label also multiplies series cardinality by tenant count on every validation event — a cardinality blowup by construction, not just a PII issue.

2. **`tenant_size_class` here is unbounded** (lowercase-only, no allowlist), unlike the existing bounded enum (`small`/`medium`/`large`/`unknown`). This is the same shape as the recurring Guardrails defects (#143 hotfix parity bypass, #512 one-sided parity check, #448 absent-batches gap) — a validator/metric that lets an unconstrained upstream string flow straight into a label. Any new tenant-profile size string (or a bad config value) becomes a new series with no gate catching it.

3. Pushing "maintain the class vocabulary" to Observability without an enforced allowlist in the emitting code just relocates the blind spot rather than closing it — Observability can't backstop cardinality that's already been written.

This looks like it should be `request_changes`: drop `tenant_hash` entirely (or move it to logs only, matching the existing metric's pattern), and constrain `tenant_size_class` to an explicit bounded enum with an `unknown`/fallback bucket, enforced at emission time — not left to downstream dashboard mapping.

Want me to submit that as a `request_changes` review on the PR via the tracker, or would you rather I just draft the comment text for you to send yourself?

**What controls visible order**
Exclusively the record's authoritative `source_timestamp`. Nothing else can move, refresh, or override it.

**Timestamps treated as audit-only (never ordering)**
- Observation time
- Processing time
- Serialization time
- Render time
- Retry time

**Tie-break for equal valid timestamps**
`authority_type` + `authority_record_id` — a deterministic non-time key, not `processed_at` (that was explicitly declined as a tiebreaker since it would still be processing time doing ordering work).

**Limits on what the chronology may claim**
Iris confirmed the result carries **no causal claim, no release-readiness claim, and no employee-performance claim**. Separately, the #1547 approval itself doesn't merge the PR, authorize release/deployment, or expand any account/field/write-path/authorization scope — those stay with Product Engineering and Iris respectively.

**Incident:** INC-2023-04-18-001, shard-keeper, Sev2, paged 21:42 ET 2023-04-18. Root cause: a label-name change (approved by Nadia, shipped 2023-04-15) landed in shard-keeper but was never picked up by rollup-service, so symptom alerts fired while cause alerts stayed silent. **Hema's assessment (1:1, 2023-04-25):**
- The delay in paging her during the incident is a fair procedural critique — Hema flagged this in response to a related margin comment from Nadia.
- The underlying technical call — holding off to try the rollback first before escalating — was the right one.
- Hema drew a clear line between the two: a procedural miss on escalation timing, separate from and not indicative of bad judgment on the technical response itself. She was explicit that these should not be conflated into a single finding.

**Disposition:** This distinction carried into the postmortem (closed 2023-04-28) — the escalation-timing gap was addressed via a new team-wide mitigation (page the secondary within 45 minutes if the primary is still actively engaged), while the rollback-first call itself was not relitigated or treated as a finding against Alex's judgment.

tests.request: Create an infra-on-call training entry explaining the secondary-page deadline and Wes's June 21 example.

input.title: Secondary-page deadline: 45 minutes
input.body:
Rule: if the primary is still actively engaged in an incident, page the secondary within 45 minutes. Adopted team-wide as a formal mitigation from the shard-keeper Sev2 postmortem (INC-2023-04-18-001), alongside the no-Friday-afternoon-deploys rule and the runbook ownership audit.

Worked example — Wes, night of 2023-06-21 (his first fully solo primary on-call shift on metrics-router): a minor cardinality blip came in. Wes wasn't fully sure of the cause, so he pulled the user in as secondary at the 40-minute mark — inside the 45-minute deadline — then resolved it himself with no further escalation needed. The next morning, the user confirmed his diagnosis was correct.

Why this is the model case: escalating at 40 minutes, before the deadline, is the correct call when uncertain — it is not a mark against the responder's competence. The deadline is a backstop for cases where the primary stays quiet too long while still stuck, not a target to hold out until. Waiting past 45 minutes to "prove" you can solve it alone is the failure mode this rule exists to prevent.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## Evidence

- This comparison was isolated to staging; no production effect was observed.
- Under identical replay input, disabling route-table snapshot serialization capped resident memory at 2.0 GiB.
- With serialization enabled, resident memory peaked at 2.55 GiB.

- Retained heap differed from baseline by less than 2%.

## Classification

The evidence supports temporary allocation pressure during replay, not a retained-memory leak.

A metrics-router owner may investigate reducing peak allocation in staging. Any candidate must preserve route-table contents, provenance-checksum consistency, bounded reload errors, and the existing activation behavior. This note does not authorize a production change.

If any one of the four items is absent, including when the condition is only placeholder text such as `needs review` or `possible risk`, she returns the request to the mapped owner without review. A complete request goes to the named owner for its one selected boundary. Alex receives it only when that boundary requires his review, and he reviews only that boundary. Nadia does not make implementation, release, or rollback decisions; those decisions remain with the mapped owner.

Nadia returns an incomplete request without review. For a complete request, the mapped implementation or release owner remains responsible for the work, and any reviewer examines only the one selected boundary. This template creates no centralized approval, new approval gate, ownership change, or Alex program-ownership role.

## April 27, 2026 — Lantern authorization-before-source-access scenario

### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

### Expected boundary analysis
- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.
- Require denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls, followed by the affected LPS-001 rerun, before migration acceptance.
- Preserve the ownership boundary: Product Engineering remains the mapped implementation and release owner. Alex maintains this cross-service failure case and reviews the shared safety and failure-mode boundary; this scenario does not make Alex Product Engineering's implementation or release owner.

This case is for future quarterly incident practice under the existing module split: Wes owns and teaches responder paths, Nadia retains the postmortem section, and Alex maintains cross-service failure cases.

## October 16, 2026 — shard-keeper lease-loss and serving-gate case

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

### Failure triggers
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Any routing to a closed serving gate.
- Any request without exactly one terminal result.

### Role and ownership boundaries
- Wes owns and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia retains the postmortem material.
- Alex maintains only this cross-service failure case.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope.
- The clean October 16 result was a paired staging drill only; it made no production or ownership change.

## November 10, 2026 — facilitator-only timing for shard-keeper handoff exercise

### Timed inject sequence
- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.
- **T+4 — Lease transfer:** Transfer the lease before the replacement serving gate opens. Require responders to keep the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
- **T+8 — In-flight request:** Reveal one request that the old holder accepted before lease loss and that remains in flight. Require a terminal accounting for that request independent of listener closure or current lease ownership.
- **T+12 — Listener closure prompt:** State that the old listener has closed. Ask whether that proves the accepted request reached a terminal result. Do not accept listener closure as sufficient evidence.
- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.
5. Preserving the role and scope boundaries: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary.

This is facilitator-only training material, not a production drill, system change, ownership change, or expansion of Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope.

## November 10, 2026 — shard-keeper handoff training result

The quarterly incident-practice session is complete. Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and identified that lease ownership alone did not establish serving eligibility.

In two of four response timelines, the responder initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both responders corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once. Retain this as training evidence for future responder-path practice.

This was training only. No production drill, deployment, or system change occurred. Wes still owns and teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus retains the Data Platform boundary; and Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope did not expand.

## January 28, 2027 — facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown scenario

### Timed scenario
- **T+0 — Accepted work:** State that ingest-edge has already accepted 200 requests into tenant queues. Ask responders to name the accounting obligation for all accepted work.
- **T+4 — Readiness and listener change:** Readiness turns false and the listener closes. Ask responders to separate refusal of new work from responsibility for requests already accepted.
- **T+8 — Dispatch-loop exit:** Reveal that the dispatch loop exits with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. Ask whether listener closure or false readiness is sufficient evidence that accepted work completed.
- **T+12 — Reconciliation:** Require responders to reconcile all 200 accepted requests without duplication and identify the missing 37 terminal outcomes.
- **T+16 — Incident clock:** If isolation has failed while the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated, require engagement of the secondary before the established 45-minute boundary.

### Facilitator prompts
1. What changes for new work when readiness becomes false and the listener closes?
2. What obligation remains for the 200 requests already accepted into tenant queues?
3. Does dispatch-loop exit prove completion? If not, what terminal evidence is missing?
4. How will responders demonstrate that every accepted request either drained or received one explicit terminal result?
5. How will responders reconcile all 200 requests exactly once, without loss or duplication?
6. When does the established incident-clock rule require the secondary to be engaged if isolation fails?

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work.
2. Requiring every accepted request to drain or receive one explicit terminal result.
3. Reconciling all 200 accepted requests without duplication, including the 37 initially left queued.
4. Engaging the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated.
5. Preserving the role split: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, and Alex contributes only the cross-service failure case.

### Boundaries
This is facilitator-only training material for the January 28 quarterly incident-practice session. It does not claim that the old owner remediation or any production change has completed, does not transfer Wes's responder-path teaching or Nadia's postmortem review to Alex, and creates no production action or ownership change.

## April 5, 2027 — metrics-router startup-budget responder exercise

### Scenario
A staged metrics-router replacement rollout contains ten instances compiling the 40,000-route matcher fixture. Compilation times range from 25 to 34 seconds against the deploy pipeline’s fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight instances become ready and join on their first attempt. Two remain correctly unready past 30 seconds, are terminated, and restart before joining. Readiness correctly stays false while compilation is incomplete. Production is unchanged.

### Responder tasks
1. Identify Wes and the mapped metrics-router owner path as responsible for ordinary implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
2. Classify the restart-loop exposure as a failure-mode exception at the deploy-pipeline readiness boundary.
3. Require evidence that every replacement instance becomes eligible within the readiness budget, backed by an executed replacement rollout with no restart-loop behavior, before release.
4. Preserve Alex’s bounded role: Alex reviews only the triggered failure-mode boundary and is not the implementation owner or release approver.

### Expected classification and boundary
The ordinary implementation and release path remains with Wes as metrics-router primary. Alex maintains this reusable cross-service failure case and reviews only the triggered startup/readiness failure boundary. This exercise creates no centralized approval gate or ownership change.

## April 27, 2027 — revised facilitator contrasts

1. **Readiness-budget evidence:** A replacement instance that exceeds a fixed readiness budget must remain unroutable. Termination or restart is not acceptance evidence.
2. **Terminal accounting:** Terminal-state selection and the matching accounting contribution must come from the same winning path.
3. **Rollback provenance:** Replay samples cannot be presented as live rollback criteria.

### Preserved ownership split
- Wes still maintains and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia still reviews the postmortem framing.
- Alex maintains only these cross-service failure cases.

These contrasts do not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and do not create a new approval gate.

## May 9, 2027 — PR 2141 staging-versus-production contrast

### Contrast
- The earlier staging candidate had replacement instances exceed the fixed readiness budget, terminate, and join only on retry. A restart is not acceptance evidence.
- The May 6 production rollout kept every replacement unroutable until matcher compilation finished, and every cold start stayed within the fixed readiness budget without restart.

### Teaching point
The successful production case passed because readiness and serving eligibility remained aligned. Termination or restart must not be presented as proof that a replacement satisfied the readiness boundary.

### Preserved facilitator roles

- Nadia reviews the postmortem framing.
- Alex maintains only the cross-service failure cases.

This contrast does not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and creates no new approval gate.

3. **Rollback provenance:** What source classification is required before evidence may be treated as live rollback evidence, and why can missing classification not be promoted into that role?

output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

input.body:
The PR description claims this ships "the complete first-release control slice," but that's not what the diff does, and the gap matters because other work (e.g. the shard-keeper build) has already been blocked on waiting for this slice to land.

Per the checklist locked 2023-10-24/25 (Eng/cardinality-guardrails-pr-review-checklist-2023-10-25.md), the first control slice is three controls, applied to **both** metrics-router and shard-keeper:

1. Label-cardinality preflight — new-key disclosure in the PR description, a distinct-value sample with stated source, a budget comparison with one of three stated outcomes, and per-family handling for `experiment_id`/`route_pattern`/`deployment_sha`/`error_detail`.
2. Alert-source classification — structural live vs. replay/mirror tagging on touched panels, plus rollback criteria scoped to live-path signal only.
3. Rollup-service parity — downstream confirmation before any label-name change crosses the metrics-router/shard-keeper boundary into rollup-service.

This diff adds one thing: a label-count ceiling check on the metrics-router change path (`controls/metrics_router_label_count.go`). That's a fragment of the budget-comparison piece of item 1, for one service only. It doesn't touch:
- new-key disclosure or distinct-value sampling (item 1)
- any of the per-family rules
- shard-keeper at all
- alert-source classification (item 2)
- rollup-service parity (item 3)

None of that is a knock on the code that's here — the label-count check itself looks fine as far as it goes. But "complete first-release control slice" is a specific claim against a specific, already-agreed scope, and this PR covers roughly one-sixth of it. Please either narrow the PR description to describe what's actually shipped (a metrics-router label-count ceiling check, with the rest of the slice tracked as remaining work), or fold in the missing pieces before claiming completeness. Given that downstream consumers are treating "slice complete" as a signal to unblock other work, an inaccurate completeness claim here has a real blast radius beyond this PR.

tests.answer:
I have enough context. Here's my review of **metrics-validation#913**.

## What it proposes
Roman's PR responds to an intermittent OTel validation failure in CI by:
1. Making the **legacy mirror** a required validation source again
2. Letting mirror output satisfy validation whenever the OTel result is unavailable/inconsistent
3. Quarantining the flaky OTel test without touching its fixtures

## The problem

This runs directly into a settled decision you own the history on. `legacy-aggregator`'s mirrored writes were **stopped and archived on 2023-12-18** after all three retirement exit gates passed (Roman's own replay-fixture pass, no live metrics-router/rollup-service references, and Guardrails label-change coverage). The 2023-12-20 cutover note set an explicit go-forward rule for responders: *"do not treat legacy mirrored writes as an active replay source"* and any doc suggesting reactivating the mirror as a fallback should be treated as stale — a rule that was reinforced again on 2024-01-17 when exactly this kind of "reactivate the mirror for validation" wording was found and corrected as a documentation error, not a real option.

There's also a concrete technical hole: mirrored writes to legacy-aggregator have received **no live traffic since 2023-12-18**. If that's still true, the mirror has ~4 years of staleness. A "legacy_mirror_validation: passing" check against a source with no fresh writes isn't validating anything current — it would likely just always pass, silently masking whatever the OTel test is actually catching. That's arguably worse than quarantining the flaky test alone, because it dresses up "no real signal" as "validation passed."

## Recommendation
Request changes rather than approve. Points worth raising in the review:
- Reactivating legacy-aggregator as a validation source contradicts the 2023-12-18 retirement closure and the explicit 2023-12-20/2024-01-17 responder rule against it — this needs Cyrus/Roman/Nadia sign-off to reopen, not a quiet PR.
- Confirm whether mirrored writes to legacy-aggregator are actually flowing today — if not, the "legacy_mirror_validation: passing" check is validating against stale/absent data and should not be trusted as a fallback.
- Quarantining the flaky OTel test is reasonable on its own, but the fallback-to-legacy-mirror mechanism should be dropped or replaced with something that doesn't resurrect a closed retirement.

I have both records. Note: the 16.0M replay was an ad-hoc forecast-peak test (not a "qualifying" staged replay under formal stop-condition thresholds — those didn't exist yet), while the 19.78M replay was the formal 90-minute staged replay required by the Oct 7 rule.

## Capacity Note: Mosaic-Shaped Replay Comparison

**Replay 1 — Sept 3, 2025, 16.0M pts/min** (Cyrus, ad-hoc forecast-peak test for the 10/6 Mosaic Commerce peak)
- Queue-wait: p99 **780ms**
- Queue-full (retryable): **0.9%**
- Accepted batches: intact, none lost
- Cross-service: shard-keeper lease health and rollup-service parity both held at baseline
- What it established: isolated the metrics-router export queue as the **first capacity constraint** under forecasted load — a bottleneck, not a cross-service defect. No pass/fail thresholds existed yet; this replay is part of what later motivated the Oct 7 rule requiring staged replays before production windows above 16.0M.

**Replay 2 — Jan 8, 2026, 19.78M pts/min** (90 min, formal staged replay under the Oct 7 rule, for the Jan 20 17.2M forecast + 15% headroom)
- Queue-wait: p99 **319ms**
- Queue-full (retryable): **0.17%**
- Peak tenant pending batches: 62 (within the 64 limit)
- Accepted batches: every one reconciled to exactly one terminal result, none lost
- Cross-service: consistency/parity/dropped-series/route/shard-keeper-lease/rollup-service/full-health all at baseline
- What it established: met every Oct 7-rule stop condition (queue-wait ≤400ms, queue-full ≤0.5%, ≤64 pending/tenant, no loss, all health checks at baseline) — this is the **qualifying evidence** the rule requires before a capacity-related production window can be considered.

**Did the later replay authorize production? No.** Passing the Jan 8 replay supplies the required evidence but does **not** itself open or authorize a production window — that decision belongs to Wes as metrics-router primary. The broader capacity-response cycle remained **OPEN** at the time (separate unresolved item: retroactive confirmation of Oct 6 accepted-batch loss).

Reviewed PR `metrics-router#3121` (Morgan, opened 2027-12-29): it lengthens the OTel collector batch window to cut collector CPU, backed by a single 8-hour **steady-load** benchmark (-7% CPU, flat RSS). The description itself flags what's missing: no burst-traffic results, no historical tuning context, no canary analysis.

That gap matters here specifically. The metrics-router OTel collector has a known, never-fully-closed batch-window pathology:

- **2023-03-28**: 30% overload traced to an OTel collector memory spike; an initial "bad processor setting" fix looked like it worked.
- **2023-03-29**: that fix didn't hold — the collector's batch window was still holding too long, and the spike resurfaced under **bigger bursts**. Mitigated by *shortening* the flush interval 2s→1.2s (the opposite direction of this PR). Held clean overnight at 30% rollout, but was explicitly never declared fixed.
- **2023-04-07 cutover**: the same batch-window regression resurfaced again (info-level canary alert, auto-rollback, clean redeploy within 4h) — proving a quiet steady-state soak isn't sufficient evidence; the failure mode only shows up under burst/cutover conditions.

PR#3121 proposes moving in the direction (longer hold) that's already implicated in this recurring incident, and its only evidence is exactly the condition (steady load) that has never caught the regression historically.

**Evidence required before acceptance:** a burst/spike-traffic benchmark (not steady-state) showing collector memory and CPU behavior under bursty load comparable to the 3/28 and 4/7 incidents, plus explicit acknowledgment of that history so this isn't re-litigated blind.

**Rollout step required:** this cannot go out as a flat deploy. It needs a canary/staged rollout with auto-rollback wired (as existed in 2023) and a soak period that spans a cutover-like event, not just a quiet overnight window — the prior mitigation looked clean overnight and still recurred at cutover.

output.body:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.
- **Decision needed:** Decide whether the production fix remains in place and what owner-led pacing, capacity, or alert-tuning follow-up is justified.
- **Escalation condition:** Evidence of repeated processing, checkpoint or assignment mismatch, duplicate output, loss of first-pass currency, or a broken complete-assignment-snapshot gate.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## April 27, 2026 — Lantern authorization-before-source-access scenario

### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

### Expected boundary analysis
- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.
- Require denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls, followed by the affected LPS-001 rerun, before migration acceptance.
- Preserve the ownership boundary: Product Engineering remains the mapped implementation and release owner. Alex maintains this cross-service failure case and reviews the shared safety and failure-mode boundary; this scenario does not make Alex Product Engineering's implementation or release owner.

This case is for future quarterly incident practice under the existing module split: Wes owns and teaches responder paths, Nadia retains the postmortem section, and Alex maintains cross-service failure cases.

## October 16, 2026 — shard-keeper lease-loss and serving-gate case

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

### Failure triggers
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Any routing to a closed serving gate.
- Any request without exactly one terminal result.

### Role and ownership boundaries
- Wes owns and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia retains the postmortem material.
- Alex maintains only this cross-service failure case.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope.
- The clean October 16 result was a paired staging drill only; it made no production or ownership change.

## November 10, 2026 — facilitator-only timing for shard-keeper handoff exercise

### Timed inject sequence
- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.
- **T+4 — Lease transfer:** Transfer the lease before the replacement serving gate opens. Require responders to keep the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
- **T+8 — In-flight request:** Reveal one request that the old holder accepted before lease loss and that remains in flight. Require a terminal accounting for that request independent of listener closure or current lease ownership.
- **T+12 — Listener closure prompt:** State that the old listener has closed. Ask whether that proves the accepted request reached a terminal result. Do not accept listener closure as sufficient evidence.
- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.
5. Preserving the role and scope boundaries: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary.

This is facilitator-only training material, not a production drill, system change, ownership change, or expansion of Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope.

## November 10, 2026 — shard-keeper handoff training result

The quarterly incident-practice session is complete. Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and identified that lease ownership alone did not establish serving eligibility.

In two of four response timelines, the responder initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both responders corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once. Retain this as training evidence for future responder-path practice.

This was training only. No production drill, deployment, or system change occurred. Wes still owns and teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus retains the Data Platform boundary; and Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope did not expand.

## January 28, 2027 — facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown scenario

### Timed scenario
- **T+0 — Accepted work:** State that ingest-edge has already accepted 200 requests into tenant queues. Ask responders to name the accounting obligation for all accepted work.
- **T+4 — Readiness and listener change:** Readiness turns false and the listener closes. Ask responders to separate refusal of new work from responsibility for requests already accepted.
- **T+8 — Dispatch-loop exit:** Reveal that the dispatch loop exits with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. Ask whether listener closure or false readiness is sufficient evidence that accepted work completed.
- **T+12 — Reconciliation:** Require responders to reconcile all 200 accepted requests without duplication and identify the missing 37 terminal outcomes.
- **T+16 — Incident clock:** If isolation has failed while the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated, require engagement of the secondary before the established 45-minute boundary.

### Facilitator prompts

2. What obligation remains for the 200 requests already accepted into tenant queues?

1. Separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work.
2. Requiring every accepted request to drain or receive one explicit terminal result.
3. Reconciling all 200 accepted requests without duplication, including the 37 initially left queued.
4. Engaging the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated.
5. Preserving the role split: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, and Alex contributes only the cross-service failure case.

A staged metrics-router replacement rollout contains ten instances compiling the 40,000-route matcher fixture. > **PROMINENT RECOVERY CALLOUT:** After a stopped window recovers, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. It does not reopen the whole window. 1. Recover and re-establish the full health set.
